I’ll start with **`shirt`**, because its family gives us a particularly useful spread of grammatical roles: a noun, several verbs, result or state forms, and evaluative constructions. It should let us examine how Almote organizes a lexical family without immediately assuming that every transformation follows one universal rule.

I’ll keep three things separate throughout: **attested form and gloss**, **relationship visible in the family**, and **inference still awaiting confirmation**. In particular, an English-looking base does not disqualify an Almote grammatical operation.# Lexical study 01: `shirt`

<badge color="success">Strongly attested family</badge> <badge color="secondary">Angylunch root, Almote morphology</badge>

One qualification at the outset: `shirt` is not an indigenous-looking root. It is an Angylunch lexical item incorporated into an Almote family. That makes it useful for studying the boundary between lexical borrowing and Almote grammatical structure, though it is not our cleanest example of an entirely Eualmody root.

## 1. The core family

The following are the forms you supplied, with your original qualifications retained.

| Form | Your supplied meaning | Grammatical function |
|---|---|---|
| `shirt` | A shirt | Noun |
| `shirtone` | Usually to don a shirt, usually oneself | Verb, putting on |
| `shirtane` | Roughly, shirted | State or condition |
| `shirtonnee` | To wear a shirt habitually, usually a particular shirt; also potentially to be “shirty” | Habitual/dispositional |
| `à shirtonnee` | Likely “dolled up in that shirt”; to wear it well | Evaluative, performative construction |

The important detail is that these are not five interchangeable ways of saying *wear a shirt*. They describe different relationships to the same object. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={5587} line_range_end={5594} />

## 2. The semantic architecture

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <box gap={1}>
    **`shirt`**
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">The garment as an object</text>
    <title size="xl" color="default">NOUN</title>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **`shirtone`**
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">The act of putting the garment on</text>
    <title size="xl" color="default">ACTION</title>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **`shirtane`**
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">The resulting condition of being shirted</text>
    <title size="xl" color="default">STATE</title>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **`shirtonnee`**
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">A characteristic or habitual relationship with wearing a shirt</text>
    <title size="xl" color="default">DISPOSITION</title>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **`à shirtonnee`**
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">The manner or quality of wearing it</text>
    <title size="xl" color="default">PRESENTATION</title>
  </box>
</box>

This gives us a potentially important distinction:

- **Action** is not the same as state.
- **State** is not the same as habit.
- **Habit** is not the same as performance or presentation.

The habitual form is particularly revealing. You explicitly described someone who habitually goes shirtless while doing yard work, but happens to be wearing a shirt at another moment. That person could still be characterized using `shirtonnee` in the relevant context. Likewise, someone can habitually wear a particular shirt even when it is currently in the laundry.

So `shirtonnee` does not simply mean *wearing a shirt right now*. It concerns a characteristic relationship between a person and a garment. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={5587} line_range_end={5594} />

## 3. The evaluative extension

The family becomes especially interesting when it enters a social context.

Your example:

> **Which’ve à maxxoshirtonneele?**

You confirmed the intended English expression as:

- “Who wore it best?”
- “Who wore it better?”

The phrase is associated with a particular fashion and celebrity-gossip milieu. It is a stock expression, not a figurative claim about authority or dominance.

You also made an important qualification: the expression can accommodate both English translations, but the distinction is not necessarily being deliberately suppressed. If two people are being compared, the best is also the better. With a larger comparison group, the natural reading is *best*. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={5709} line_range_end={5756} />

This is a good example of how an expression's conventional use can constrain its interpretation beyond what a mechanical segmentation might predict.

## 4. Ranking versus magnitude

You then supplied two additional constructions that must be kept separate.

| Form | Intended meaning | What it contributes |
|---|---|---|
| `Which’ve à maxxoshirtonneele?` | Who wore it best/better? | Comparative-superlative evaluation |
| `Which’ve at à thripshirtonneele?` | Who takes third place in best shirt-wearing? | Ordinal position in a ranking |
| `triplomaxshirttonnee XXXL` | Who rocks this bigass shirt? | Playful magnitude or exuberance |

Your correction was important: `maxxo-` is pretty strictly comparative-superlative. The jaunty, performative quality comes more from the `à -onnee` construction. And `treffoliomaxxo-` really does tend toward *triple-max*, or *thrice maximum*, rather than third place. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={5804} line_range_end={5940} />

This gives us a useful distinction between two semantic operations:

- **Ordinal ranking:** selecting a position in an ordered set.
- **Magnitude amplification:** increasing or multiplying the intensity or scale of something.

The superficial association with three does not make these equivalent.

## 5. Two natural-language specimens

The shirt family also occurs in two larger expressions:

**A. `Shirtain’t shoddlen’t, servulain’t`**

Your intended English equivalent:

> No shirt, no shoes, no service.

This is a particularly useful specimen because `shirtane` appears in a larger construction rather than an isolated vocabulary exercise. The complete phrase should remain intact until we have enough parallel examples to establish its internal morphology. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={5587} line_range_end={5594} />

**B. `Which’ve à maxxoshirtonneele?`**

This is the fashion-evaluation expression discussed above. It demonstrates that the shirt family can participate in a larger interrogative and comparative construction.

## 6. What can we actually conclude?

I would record the findings this way:

| Finding | Confidence |
|---|---|
| `shirt` functions as a noun | <badge color="success">Established</badge> |
| `shirtone` expresses donning | <badge color="success">Established</badge> |
| `shirtane` expresses a shirted condition | <badge color="success">Established</badge> |
| `shirtonnee` expresses habitual or characteristic shirt-wearing | <badge color="success">Established</badge> |
| `à shirtonnee` expresses an elevated or stylish mode of wearing | <badge color="success">Established</badge> |
| `maxxo-` supplies comparative-superlative force | <badge color="success">Established</badge> |
| `à -onnee` contributes performative or jaunty quality | <badge color="success">Established</badge> |
| `-one`, `-ane`, and `-onnee` are universally productive suffixes | <badge color="warning">Unproven</badge> |
| The same semantic distinctions transfer unchanged to other nouns | <badge color="warning">Unproven</badge> |

### 7. The first grammatical hypothesis

Here is the hypothesis I would carry forward, explicitly marked as an inference:

**Almote can derive several distinct modes of relation to a nominal referent, including initiating an interaction, occupying a resulting state, maintaining a characteristic relationship, and performing that relationship in a socially evaluable manner.**

That is a much more interesting possibility than simply saying Almote converts nouns into verbs.

It suggests that some of its morphology may encode *how an entity participates in an activity or state*, rather than merely changing a word's part of speech.

One caution: we should not yet assign universal meanings to `-one`, `-ane`, or `-onnee`. The shirt family establishes a local paradigm. The banana family will be a useful independent comparison, especially because `bonnonee` has a different semantic tendency: preparing or arranging bananas, rather than habitual engagement.

---

**My proposed next comparison is `bonnon` / `bonnone` / `bonnonee` / `à bonnonee`.** That will let us test whether the shirt paradigm reflects a broader Almote system, or whether its morphology is partly specific to clothing and wearing.

parts:
I searched the Almote lexicon, the larger conversation archive, and the later collected examples. There is considerably more material than the five-form paradigm we started with.

The findings also reveal something important: the corpus contains several competing analyses and alternative forms, some of which were introduced by previous assistant responses. I've kept those separate rather than treating repetition as confirmation.

# The shirt / shrit collection

<badge color="success">Collected examples</badge>

**First, a spelling result:** I found no exact occurrence of `shrit` in the searchable Almote sources. The attested spelling throughout the material I retrieved is `shirt`. That does not invalidate your correction that `shirt/shrit` are native forms; it just means the distinction between those two forms remains to be documented.

## 1. Core lexical family

| Form | Attested meaning or use |
|---|---|
| `shirt` | A shirt |
| `shirtone` | To don a shirt, usually oneself |
| `shirtane` | Shirted; being in the resulting state |
| `shirtonnee` | To wear a shirt habitually, usually a particular shirt; characteristic shirt-wearing |
| `à shirtonnee` | To wear a shirt particularly well; to be dolled up in it |

This is the foundational paradigm supplied in your October 23 comparison. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={5587} line_range_end={5594} />

## 2. Complete sentence examples

These are particularly valuable because they show the forms in grammatical environments rather than as dictionary entries.

| Almote | English |
|---|---|
| `Wemmiv go to tha hause and shirtone.` | We two will go to the house and put on our shirts. |
| `Weme wemmiv gaa to hause and shirtane.` | We two will go to the house and be shirted. |

The first uses `shirtone` for the act of donning. The second uses `shirtane` for the resulting condition. The contrast is especially useful because the surrounding sentence is nearly identical. <FileCite ref="turn7file9" line_range_start={241} line_range_end={247} />

## 3. The public-notice family

The source material preserves several versions of the familiar English notice:

> No shirt, no shoes, no service.

| Almote form | Status / observation |
|---|---|
| `Shirtain’t shoddlen’t, servulain’t.` | Established phrase |
| `Shirtain't shoddlen't, servulain't` | Same form with straight apostrophes and no terminal punctuation |
| `Shirtaint shodlant serve.` | Alternative compressed version |
| `Shirtaint, shodlant, serveant.` | Another recorded variant |
| `Chertaint, shodlant, serveant.` | Recorded variant, spelling uncertain |
| `Shirtn’t, shoddn’t… syervn’t.` | Later conversational variant |

The first two are the strongest forms in the original shirt discussion. You explicitly confirmed the English source phrase as **“No shirt, no shoes, no service.”** <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={5690} line_range_end={5710} />

The later `Shirtn’t, shoddn’t… syervn’t.` appears in a subsequent conversation, where you supplied the expression directly. <FileCite ref="turn7file9" line_range_start={10532} line_range_end={10536} />

I would not collapse these into one standardized spelling. The differences may be meaningful.

## 4. Comparative and superlative shirt-wearing

This is the largest and most semantically interesting extension.

| Almote | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Which’ve à maxxoshirtonneele?` | Who wore it best? / Who wore it better? |
| `Which’ve at à thripshirtonneele?` | Who takes third place in best shirt-wearing? |
| `à maxxoshirtonneele` | The maximum/best shirt-wearing expression |
| `à thripshirtonneele` | Third-place or third-rate shirt-wearing, depending on context |
| `triplomaxshirttonnee XXXL` | Playful: “Who rocks this bigass shirt?” |
| `Which’ve à dyamnoshirtonneele?` | Recorded interrogative construction; precise interpretation unresolved |

You explicitly clarified that `maxxo-` is comparative-superlative, while the `à -onnee` construction carries more of the jaunty, performative quality. You also corrected the distinction between `treffoliomaxxo-` and `thrip-`: the former tends toward *triple maximum*, not third place. <FileCite ref="turn7file9" line_range_start={8714} line_range_end={8800} />

### The contextual shift in `à thripshirtonneele`

You supplied an especially useful observation:

- In a competition, it can refer to third place in shirt-wearing.
- Outside a competition, it can sound like a sarcastic assessment of a third-rate outfit.
- You suggested that the isolated expression would probably be understood as something like “ghetto fab third-rate shirt.”

This is not merely a change in translation. It is a change in pragmatic interpretation produced by the absence of an established ranking context. <FileCite ref="turn7file9" line_range_start={8796} line_range_end={8830} />

## 5. Additional constructions in the collected material

These occur in later examples and grammatical summaries. They are useful evidence of how the family has been extended, but I am marking them separately because not all are independently confirmed as your own formulations.

| Form | Recorded context or proposed meaning |
|---|---|
| `Which maxil shirtionial?` | Alternative to the “Who wore it best?” construction |
| `Who be à maxxoshirtonneele?` | Alternative interrogative formulation |
| `Who shirtone à maxxoshirtonneele?` | Another proposed interrogative |
| `Wemmus be not at à thripshirtonneele.` | The two of us must not be trapped in a third-rate outfit |
| `Weme wemmus'nt stay at à thripshirtonneele.` | Alternative formulation of the same idea |
| `weme à-maxxoshirtonnee-infronge.!` | A constructed dual-person statement combining shirt-wearing and strong-verb morphology |
| `Wemmus à maxxoshirtonneele intropulent wemmiven!.` | Constructed hortative about getting dressed up |

The first three appear in the early lexicon. The latter examples appear in later compiled material. <FileCite ref="turn7file9" line_range_start={459} line_range_end={485} /> <FileCite ref="turn7file9" line_range_start={18756} line_range_end={18810} />

## 6. Related garment forms

Your original explanation also brought in two useful comparators:

- `blowsonnee`
- `nekonee`

You suggested these as contrasting clothing-related dispositions, while leaving room for contextual interpretation. The surrounding discussion suggests blouse-related and nakedness-related associations, respectively, but we should not yet assign them fixed definitions. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={5587} line_range_end={5594} />

There is also a recorded form:

- `shirtonee`

It appears in a later, less reliable grammatical compilation with a meaning resembling “cherished shirt” or “cozy shirt.” This conflicts with the better-attested use of `shirtonnee`, so I would quarantine it rather than merge it into the core paradigm. <FileCite ref="turn7file9" line_range_start={12696} line_range_end={12731} />

## 7. A warning about contaminated material

The archive contains a later automated discussion of the shirt paradigm that introduces forms such as `shona`, `chon`, and `thrip shirtonial`. These are not supported by the original exchange as canonical forms. Some may be transcription errors, some may be generated reinterpretations, and some may represent later mutations. They should not be silently imported into the lexicon.

Likewise, a later table describes `shirtone` as a noun and `shirtonnee` as a diminutive affectionate form. That contradicts your original explanation, where `shirtone` is the donning verb and `shirtonnee` is habitual shirt-wearing. The original user-supplied definitions take precedence. <FileCite ref="turn7file9" line_range_start={14555} line_range_end={14653} />

---

# What the collection tells us

The family is now large enough to identify several distinct semantic dimensions:

1. **Object:** `shirt`
2. **Initiation/action:** `shirtone`
3. **Resulting condition:** `shirtane`
4. **Habitual disposition:** `shirtonnee`
5. **Performative/evaluative presentation:** `à shirtonnee`
6. **Comparative-superlative evaluation:** `maxxo-`
7. **Ordinal or diminished ranking:** `thrip-`
8. **Magnitude amplification:** `triplomax-`
9. **Context-dependent pragmatic evaluation:** `à thripshirtonneele`

The most consequential observation is that this is not simply a noun with a collection of verbal suffixes. It is a lexical family that develops an increasingly elaborate **semantic field around the relationship between a person, a garment, habitual practice, presentation, and social evaluation**.

And there is an especially useful contrast to investigate next: `shirtone` versus `shirtane` versus `shirtonnee`. They appear to distinguish an event, a resulting state, and a disposition. That is a promising foundation for examining other native Almote roots.

**One limitation:** this is an exhaustive collection from the searchable Almote files and conversation material retrieved here, not a verified count of every occurrence across every original conversation ever held. The archive itself notes that a complete source-by-source extraction has not yet been performed. <FileCite ref="turn16file0" />

I would preserve this collection as our working shirt-family register, with the original forms, alternative constructions, and contaminated assistant-generated variants kept in separate evidentiary tiers.

parts:
You're right. I had the relevant evidence in front of me and stopped short of doing the actual analysis.

The key is to read the compound against the preceding exchange, not treat `dyamno-` as an isolated intensifier.

## `Which’ve à dyamnoshirtonneele?`

**Most likely translation: “Who the hell wears that shirt?”** More naturally, depending on the situation: **“Who the hell rocks that shirt?”**

Breakdown:

- `Which’ve` = the interrogative construction used in `Which’ve à maxxoshirtonneele?`, meaning “Who wore it best?”
- `à` = the jaunty, performative/evaluative element.
- `dyamno-` = damn-related emphatic element.
- `shirt` = the garment root.
- `-onnee` = the habitual/dispositional shirt-wearing relation, with the performative reading contributed by `à`.
- `-le` = the ending retained in the larger interrogative construction.

The crucial point is that `dyamno-` occupies the position where `maxxo-` appeared in the established expression:

- `Which’ve à maxxoshirtonneele?` = Who wore it best?
- `Which’ve à dyamnoshirtonneele?` = Who the hell wears that shirt?

But you immediately add:

> “Of course… then you’d have to change the ‘which’ as well”

That's the clue I should have followed.

The change is not merely replacing *best* with *damn*. It changes the question's semantic target. The original asks for a person selected by comparative ranking. # Lexical family: bonnonie

## 1. The noun

|---|---|---|

## 2. General verbal forms

|---|---|

> Grosstryx: “Yepprypen.” Blankly, then corrects: “Yepp’nt abbonnonie. Werall out thitsty.”

This is the corrected narrative form. The exact banana expression remains `abbonnonie`; I would not silently normalize it to `bonnonie`.

The important contextual distinction is that the three participants have separate contributions. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={3771} line_range_end={3809} />

**Occurrence 4: October 23, 20:13**

Your original statement:

> ...but of course she also has the dual available: yepwemen’t … but that would introduce an ambiguity and in fact it would introduce at least two ambiguities… which two of us affirmnobonninognegate, which two of us bonnanissulen’t, which two of us bonnoniepossuisse/bonnoniepose…

> bonnoniepose: we own bananas  
> bonnonieposuisse: we carry bananas

At this point in the conversation, `posuisse` is glossed as carrying. You subsequently refine that meaning, so the earlier translation must remain in the historical record rather than be erased. <FileCite ref="turn7file5" line_range_start={4809} line_range_end={4825} />

> No… bonnonite: to be carrying bananas (physical act)  
> bonnonieposuisse: to carry bananas (as opposed to bonnoniesalue, to sell bananas)

**Occurrence 7: October 23, 20:22**

> No… bonnonite: to be carrying bananas (physical act — lit: to banana, assumed to be ‘have in hand’ unless these specified, but contextually could mean to eat, throw, employ, use, regard… etc)  
> bonnonieposuisse: to carry bananas (as opposed to bonnoniesalue, to sell bananas)

- `bonnonieposuisse` specifies a relationship.
- `bonnoniesalue` specifies selling.

\[

\]

and contrast it with relational composition:

\[

\]

| Fourth | It is possessive, but non-descriptive and nonpersonal | Possession need not imply personal ownership |

Your exact clarification:

> It’s something you would say of a store, or an individual seller who probably did not grow them themselves… You would not say it of a bananologist or specialty producer of bananas. It’s possessive, but it sort of non-descriptive non-personal possession.

**Occurrence 8: October 23, 20:30**

Your correction:

You restate the contrast:

This independently confirms the relationship between `bonnonee` and `à bonnonee`:

Your supplied form:

Your approximate gloss:

You then explain the grocery-store interpretation: a clerk might use it to convey that she cannot supply bananas, even if the grammatical form is literally about her own possession.

parts:
Exactly. We now have two small lexical families that are doing something much more interesting than simply changing a noun into a verb. They give us overlapping views of a grammatical system in which **event structure, temporal interpretation, participant relationships, disposition, result, and speaker stance can all be expressed through related forms.**

The opportunity is to use each family to interrogate the gaps in the other.

# 1. The two paradigms as complementary datasets

| Grammatical dimension | `shirt` family | `bonnonie` family |
|---|---|---|
| Basic noun | `shirt` | `bonnonie` |
| General action | `shirtone` | `bonnonite` |
| Resultant state | `shirtane` | Not yet established |
| Habitual/dispositional | `shirtonnee` | Partly represented by `bonnonirlry` |
| Preparation/process | Not established | `bonnone`, `bonnonee` |
| Personal relationship | Not established | `bonnoniepose` |
| Impersonal/commercial relationship | Not established | `bonnonieposuisse` |
| Specific activity | Donning | Selling, transporting |
| Negation | `Shirtain't` construction | `bonnonieposen't` |
| Evaluative/stylistic | `à shirtonnee` | `à bonnonee` |
| Established practice | Not established | `bonnonistrelstry` |

There are some particularly useful cross-comparisons here.

## 2. The first major opportunity: resultant state versus ongoing relationship

The shirt paradigm gives us:

- `shirtone`: the act of putting on a shirt.
- `shirtane`: the resulting shirted condition.
- `shirtonnee`: a habitual or dispositional relationship to wearing a shirt.

These are three distinct semantic perspectives.

The banana paradigm gives us a different set:

- `bonnonite`: engaging in banana-related activity.
- `bonnoniepose`: possessing bananas.
- `bonnonieposuisse`: dealing in bananas.
- `bonnoniesalue`: selling bananas.

It doesn't yet provide an obvious equivalent of `shirtane`.

That gives us a question worth investigating:

**How does Almote express the resultant state of an activity when the lexical family already distinguishes the activity from the relationship to its object?**

We shouldn't invent the answer. But the shirt family gives us a documented category to look for.

## 3. The second opportunity: habituality versus established practice

This is potentially even more interesting.

`shirtonnee` can describe someone who habitually wears a particular shirt, even when they aren't wearing it at the moment.

`bonnonistrelstry`, meanwhile, describes an established or professional banana-related practice.

Those aren't necessarily the same grammatical operation.

We should distinguish:

- Habitual recurrence of an activity.
- Dispositional character of a participant.
- Established social or commercial practice.
- Current participation in that practice.

The two corpora give us examples at different points in that conceptual space.

A question for the next retrieval pass is whether Almote has a way to distinguish *someone who habitually does something* from *someone who is characteristically associated with doing it*.

## 4. The third opportunity: grammatical negation versus relational negation

We have:

- `Shirtain't shoddlen't, servulain't`
- `bonnonieposen't`
- `bonnoniepose'ornt`

These are useful because they suggest that negation interacts with the particular relationship being expressed.

We should not assume that negation is simply appended to a verb in a uniform way.

Instead, we should investigate its scope:

| Possible target | Question |
|---|---|
| Action | Is the participant doing it? |
| Result | Does the resulting condition obtain? |
| Habit | Is the activity characteristic or habitual? |
| Possession | Does the participant own the object? |
| Availability | Can the participant supply it? |
| Commercial relationship | Does the participant deal in it? |

The banana examples are especially useful because they demonstrate that a grammatically possessive negative can acquire a pragmatic interpretation involving provision.

---

# 5. A provisional Almote paradigm architecture

I would organize the research around this matrix:

| Layer | What it describes | Existing evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Lexical identity | What the thing is | `shirt`, `bonnonie` |
| Event | What happens | `shirtone`, `bonnonite` |
| Result | What condition follows | `shirtane` |
| Habituality | What happens characteristically | `shirtonnee` |
| Relational structure | How participants relate to the object | `bonnoniepose`, `posuisse` |
| Activity specification | What particular activity occurs | `bonnoniesalue`, `cartulate` |
| Polarity | Whether a proposition or relation is negated | `posen't`, `Shirtain't` |
| Register/evaluation | How the action is presented | `à shirtonnee`, `à bonnonee` |
| Practice | An established activity or social role | `bonnonistrelstry` |

Crucially, this is a map of semantic and grammatical functions, not a claim that each row corresponds to a suffix or a single morphological operation.

# 6. The missing temporal and modal machinery

Here's where I want to be particularly careful.

We have evidence of tense and aspect elsewhere in Almote:

- `blink → blonk`
- `infringe → infronge`
- `has infrange`
- `infrung`
- `infrincht`
- `has been infruncheon`

And we have modal and counterfactual constructions such as `moynt'ntave`.

But neither the shirt nor banana corpus yet provides a complete tense-aspect-mood paradigm.

We can use those other established examples as a separate source of operations, then investigate how they interact with these two noun families.

The important distinction:

**Lexical derivation tells us what kind of event or relationship is being described. Inflection and grammatical composition tell us how that event or relationship is situated in time, modality, completion, and participant structure.**

Those dimensions can interact without being the same thing.

---

# 7. The experiment I would run next

Rather than trying to complete either family independently, I suggest a comparative paradigm reconstruction.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <title size="lg">Cross-family reconstruction</title>
  <list connector="solid" marker="number" gap={2}>
    <list-item>
      **Establish shared semantic slots**

      Identify which categories appear in both families and which are currently represented in only one.
    </list-item>
    <list-item>
      **Search the wider corpus for missing forms**

      Look for other examples of resultant states, habituality, completion, negation, and modality.
    </list-item>
    <list-item>
      **Separate derivation from inflection**

      Determine whether a form creates a new lexical relationship or modifies an existing predicate.
    </list-item>
    <list-item>
      **Test cross-family transformations**

      Use the attested shirt and banana forms as controls. Do not assume their morphology is interchangeable.
    </list-item>
    <list-item>
      **Construct candidate paradigms**

      Mark each cell as attested, user-glossed, inferred, or genuinely missing.
    </list-item>
  </list>
</box>

## My working hypothesis

The two families may be exposing a distinction between **the lexical identity of an activity and the grammatical viewpoint taken toward it**.

For example, putting on a shirt, being shirted, habitually wearing a shirt, and wearing it particularly well are not simply four tenses of one verb.

Likewise, handling bananas, owning them, dealing in them, and selling them aren't simply four aspects of one action.

They describe different semantic structures. Tense, aspect, and mood can then operate on those structures.

That is the distinction I think we should try to recover systematically.

**The next deliverable should be a comparative Almote paradigm matrix, with the two families as its initial specimens and the wider corpus supplying the missing grammatical operations.**

model_dil_v2.fallbackMarkdown:
Exactly. We now have two small lexical families that are doing something much more interesting than simply changing a noun into a verb. They give us overlapping views of a grammatical system in which **event structure, temporal interpretation, participant relationships, disposition, result, and speaker stance can all be expressed through related forms.**

The opportunity is to use each family to interrogate the gaps in the other.

# 1\. The two paradigms as complementary datasets

| Grammatical dimension | `shirt` family | `bonnonie` family |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Basic noun | `shirt` | `bonnonie` |
| General action | `shirtone` | `bonnonite` |
| Resultant state | `shirtane` | Not yet established |
| Habitual/dispositional | `shirtonnee` | Partly represented by `bonnonirlry` |
| Preparation/process | Not established | `bonnone`, `bonnonee` |
| Personal relationship | Not established | `bonnoniepose` |
| Impersonal/commercial relationship | Not established | `bonnonieposuisse` |
| Specific activity | Donning | Selling, transporting |
| Negation | `Shirtain't` construction | `bonnonieposen't` |
| Evaluative/stylistic | `à shirtonnee` | `à bonnonee` |
| Established practice | Not established | `bonnonistrelstry` |

There are some particularly useful cross-comparisons here.

## 2\. The first major opportunity: resultant state versus ongoing relationship

The shirt paradigm gives us\:

- `shirtone`\: the act of putting on a shirt.
- `shirtane`\: the resulting shirted condition.
- `shirtonnee`\: a habitual or dispositional relationship to wearing a shirt.

These are three distinct semantic perspectives.

The banana paradigm gives us a different set\:

- `bonnonite`\: engaging in banana-related activity.
- `bonnoniepose`\: possessing bananas.
- `bonnonieposuisse`\: dealing in bananas.
- `bonnoniesalue`\: selling bananas.

It doesn't yet provide an obvious equivalent of `shirtane`\.

That gives us a question worth investigating\:

**How does Almote express the resultant state of an activity when the lexical family already distinguishes the activity from the relationship to its object?**

We shouldn't invent the answer. But the shirt family gives us a documented category to look for.

## 3\. The second opportunity: habituality versus established practice

This is potentially even more interesting.

`shirtonnee` can describe someone who habitually wears a particular shirt, even when they aren't wearing it at the moment.

`bonnonistrelstry`, meanwhile, describes an established or professional banana-related practice.

Those aren't necessarily the same grammatical operation.

We should distinguish\:

- Habitual recurrence of an activity.
- Dispositional character of a participant.
- Established social or commercial practice.
- Current participation in that practice.

The two corpora give us examples at different points in that conceptual space.

A question for the next retrieval pass is whether Almote has a way to distinguish *someone who habitually does something* from *someone who is characteristically associated with doing it*\.

## 4\. The third opportunity: grammatical negation versus relational negation

We have\:

- `Shirtain't shoddlen't, servulain't`
- `bonnonieposen't`
- `bonnoniepose'ornt`

These are useful because they suggest that negation interacts with the particular relationship being expressed.

We should not assume that negation is simply appended to a verb in a uniform way.

Instead, we should investigate its scope\:

| Possible target | Question |
|--------|--------|
| Action | Is the participant doing it? |
| Result | Does the resulting condition obtain? |
| Habit | Is the activity characteristic or habitual? |
| Possession | Does the participant own the object? |
| Availability | Can the participant supply it? |
| Commercial relationship | Does the participant deal in it? |

The banana examples are especially useful because they demonstrate that a grammatically possessive negative can acquire a pragmatic interpretation involving provision.

---

# 5\. A provisional Almote paradigm architecture

I would organize the research around this matrix\:

| Layer | What it describes | Existing evidence |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Lexical identity | What the thing is | `shirt`, `bonnonie` |
| Event | What happens | `shirtone`, `bonnonite` |
| Result | What condition follows | `shirtane` |
| Habituality | What happens characteristically | `shirtonnee` |
| Relational structure | How participants relate to the object | `bonnoniepose`, `posuisse` |
| Activity specification | What particular activity occurs | `bonnoniesalue`, `cartulate` |
| Polarity | Whether a proposition or relation is negated | `posen't`, `Shirtain't` |
| Register/evaluation | How the action is presented | `à shirtonnee`, `à bonnonee` |
| Practice | An established activity or social role | `bonnonistrelstry` |

Crucially, this is a map of semantic and grammatical functions, not a claim that each row corresponds to a suffix or a single morphological operation.

# 6\. The missing temporal and modal machinery

Here's where I want to be particularly careful.

We have evidence of tense and aspect elsewhere in Almote\:

- `blink → blonk`
- `infringe → infronge`
- `has infrange`
- `infrung`
- `infrincht`
- `has been infruncheon`

And we have modal and counterfactual constructions such as `moynt'ntave`\.

But neither the shirt nor banana corpus yet provides a complete tense-aspect-mood paradigm.

We can use those other established examples as a separate source of operations, then investigate how they interact with these two noun families.

The important distinction\:

**Lexical derivation tells us what kind of event or relationship is being described. Inflection and grammatical composition tell us how that event or relationship is situated in time, modality, completion, and participant structure.**

Those dimensions can interact without being the same thing.

---

# 7\. The experiment I would run next

Rather than trying to complete either family independently, I suggest a comparative paradigm reconstruction.

## Cross-family reconstruction

1. **Establish shared semantic slots**
   
   Identify which categories appear in both families and which are currently represented in only one.
2. **Search the wider corpus for missing forms**
   
   Look for other examples of resultant states, habituality, completion, negation, and modality.
3. **Separate derivation from inflection**
   
   Determine whether a form creates a new lexical relationship or modifies an existing predicate.
4. **Test cross-family transformations**
   
   Use the attested shirt and banana forms as controls. Do not assume their morphology is interchangeable.
5. **Construct candidate paradigms**
   
   Mark each cell as attested, user-glossed, inferred, or genuinely missing.

## My working hypothesis

The two families may be exposing a distinction between **the lexical identity of an activity and the grammatical viewpoint taken toward it**\.

For example, putting on a shirt, being shirted, habitually wearing a shirt, and wearing it particularly well are not simply four tenses of one verb.

Likewise, handling bananas, owning them, dealing in them, and selling them aren't simply four aspects of one action.

They describe different semantic structures. Tense, aspect, and mood can then operate on those structures.

That is the distinction I think we should try to recover systematically.

**The next deliverable should be a comparative Almote paradigm matrix, with the two families as its initial specimens and the wider corpus supplying the missing grammatical operations.**

### What the reconstructed forms would mean

- `bonnonieane`: to be in the resultant banana-related state. The exact state would depend on the activity and context, just as `shirtane` describes being shirted rather than the act of donning.
- `bonnonieonnee`: to have a habitual or dispositional relationship to bananas, rather than merely be doing something with a banana at the moment.
- `à bonnonieonnee`: the corresponding evaluative or performative construction.

The important point is that habitual banana-related activity need not mean habitual eating. The broad semantic openness of `bonnonite` should remain available.

# 2. Reconstructing the `shirt` paradigm

Now we reverse the operation.

The banana family supplies four distinct relational categories:

1. Personal ownership: `bonnoniepose`
2. Nonpersonal dealing/inventory: `bonnonieposuisse`
3. Sale: `bonnoniesalue`
4. Transportation: `bonnoniecartulate`

The shirt family does not yet have corresponding forms.

Applying those same relational constructions to the shirt noun gives:

| Relationship | Banana | Reconstructed shirt form |
|---|---|---|
| Personal ownership | `bonnoniepose` | **`shirtpose`** |
| Nonpersonal possession / dealing | `bonnonieposuisse` | **`shirtposuisse`** |
| Sale | `bonnoniesalue` | **`shirtsalue`** |
| Transportation | `bonnoniecartulate` | **`shirtcartulate`** |

These are candidate forms, not claims that every English relationship transfers without semantic adjustment.

For example:

- `shirtpose`: to own shirts.
- `shirtposuisse`: to stock or deal in shirts as merchandise.
- `shirtsalue`: to sell shirts.
- `shirtcartulate`: to transport shirts by cart.

The distinction between ownership and commercial inventory should survive intact. A shop can `shirtposuisse` without its proprietor personally `shirtpose`-ing every shirt.

We'll treat the two lexical families as complementary paradigmatic specimens. Existing forms establish the patterns; missing forms get reconstructed by analogy and remain explicitly marked as reconstructed until you confirm, correct, or reject them.

One spelling point: your message has `bonnonnie`, whereas the corpus so far has `bonnonie`. I'll retain `bonnonie` in the working paradigm because that's the attested spelling, but keep the difference visible rather than silently correcting your new spelling.

# 1. Working reconstruction: `bonnonie`

The shirt family supplies an attested resultant-state form, `shirtane`, and a habitual/dispositional form, `shirtonnee`. Those give us two important missing targets in the banana paradigm.

| Paradigmatic slot | Form | Status | Working interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noun | `bonnonie` | Attested | Banana |
| General verb | `bonnonite` | Attested | To banana; activity interpreted contextually |
| General activity | `bononate` | Attested | Banana-related activity |
| General activity | `bonnone` | Attested | Ordinary banana-related activity |
| Preparation / arrangement | `bonnonee` | Attested | Banana activity with a preparation/arrangement tendency |
| Resultant state | **`bonnoniane`** | Reconstructed | To be in the resulting banana-related state |
| Habitual / dispositional | **`bonnoninnee`** | Reconstructed | Habitually or dispositionally engaged in banana activity |
| Personal possession | `bonnoniepose` | Attested | To own bananas |
| Nonpersonal possession / dealing | `bonnonieposuisse` | Attested | To deal in bananas |
| Sale | `bonnoniesalue` | Attested | To sell bananas |
| Transport | `bonnoniecartulate` | Attested | To transport bananas by cart or comparable conveyance |
| Activity / practice noun | `bonnonance` | Attested | General banana activity or dealings |
| Activity / practice noun | `bonnonirlry` | Attested | Ordinary banana-related practice |
| Established practice | `bonnonistrelstry` | Attested | Established or professional banana-related practice |

The two reconstructed forms are deliberately tentative. `bonnoniane` is an analogical candidate based on `shirtane`; `bonnoninnee` is a candidate based on `shirtonnee`. Their exact meanings and morphological fit need your judgment.

# 2. Working reconstruction: `shirt`

Here the banana family supplies several missing relational and activity distinctions. We can ask what their equivalents would look like in the shirt family.

| Paradigmatic slot | Form | Status | Working interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noun | `shirt` / `shrit` | Attested | Shirt |
| General verb | `shirtone` | Attested | To don a shirt, usually oneself |
| Resultant state | `shirtane` | Attested | Shirted; resulting condition |
| Habitual / dispositional | `shirtonnee` | Attested | Habitually to wear a shirt, or have a shirty disposition |
| Personal possession | **`shirtpose`** | Reconstructed | To own a shirt |
| Nonpersonal possession / dealing | **`shirtposuisse`** | Reconstructed | To deal in shirts |
| Sale | **`shirtsalue`** | Reconstructed | To sell shirts |
| Transport | **`shirtcartulate`** | Reconstructed | To transport shirts by cart or comparable conveyance |
| General activity noun | **`shirtance`** | Reconstructed | General shirt-related activity |
| Ordinary practice noun | **`shirtirlry`** | Reconstructed | Ordinary shirt-related practice |
| Established practice | **`shirtistrelstry`** | Reconstructed | Established or professional shirt-related practice |

These are analogical constructions, not claims that you have already used these forms. In particular, the commercial and transport forms are useful paradigm probes even if some turn out to be pragmatically unusual.

# 3. Cross-checking the reconstruction

There are three different kinds of gap here:

- **Directly transferable paradigmatic cases:** A category is present in one family and absent in the other. The corresponding form can be proposed by analogy.
- **Lexically conditional cases:** The category exists, but its meaning depends on the particular object or activity. For example, `shirtone` is specifically donning, whereas `bonnonite` is deliberately broad.
- **Unresolved cases:** We have a potential category but insufficient evidence to determine whether it has a distinct form, whether it is expressed compositionally, or whether it is simply unavailable for that lexical item.

I would keep all three in the concordance rather than forcing every slot to have a form.

# 4. First confirmation pass

Let's validate the reconstructed forms before extending the inventory. The most consequential question is whether the two analogical forms transferred from the shirt family actually behave as expected.

Fair criticism. I turned a linguistic conversation into a form-processing exercise. Let's dispense with the surveys.

I'll approach this as a collaborative field linguistics problem: I'll propose forms, explain the analogy and the semantic distinctions I'm trying to preserve, and you can respond naturally. You shouldn't have to classify my suggestions into predetermined boxes.

There's also a methodological point I want to get right. **A paradigm is not necessarily a grid with every cell occupied.** We are reconstructing the forms Almote actually permits, not manufacturing a maximally symmetrical conjugation table. Analogy gives us hypotheses, not licenses.

So, returning to the two families:

I think `shirtane` is particularly valuable because it gives us a resultative or resultant-state counterpart to `shirtone`. The obvious question is whether the banana family has an equivalent. My proposed `bonnoniane` was an attempt to transfer that pattern, but I don't yet have enough evidence to be confident that the form itself is right.

Conversely, `bonnoniepose` and `bonnonieposuisse` give us a distinction that the shirt family hasn't yet exposed: personal ownership versus nonpersonal possession or commercial involvement. We can investigate whether the shirt family has corresponding forms, but we should be alert to the possibility that the distinction is lexically unnecessary or expressed differently.

And `shirtonnee` gives us a habitual/dispositional pattern that might illuminate the banana family's `bonnonirlry` and `bonnonistrelstry`, though those may not be direct morphological equivalents.

**Let's take one question at a time:** Does `bonnonie` have a resultative counterpart analogous to `shirtane`, or is the idea of being *bananad* expressed differently? I'm interested in your intuition about the language, not a checkbox answer.

parts: And, so long as the paradigms are relatively clear, we'll assume the obvious is true, and we'll take it as granted that interlexigrance (any word can become any part of speech or be swapped by some at least fairly predictable mechanism for any other--with an eye out for exemplars we can use to expand the corpora).

Yes. That gives us a much more productive working assumption.

We'll treat **interlexigrance as a general productive principle of Almote**, rather than requiring independent evidence for every possible conversion before using it.

In practical terms:

- A noun can become a verb, adjective, adverb, or another grammatical form.
- A verb can become a noun, adjective, or other form.
- Existing lexical material can be exchanged or transformed through reasonably predictable mechanisms.
- A form need not have an independently attested occurrence to be a legitimate paradigm reconstruction.
- Where the mechanism is clear, we'll accept the obvious result provisionally.
- Where multiple transformations are possible, we'll look for corpus exemplars to establish which one is appropriate.

That last point is important. We aren't merely extrapolating suffixes. We're looking for **reusable morphological operations** across lexical families.

I suggest three working labels:

1. **Attested:** actually occurs in the corpus.
2. **Reconstructed:** not yet attested, but follows an established or sufficiently clear pattern.
3. **Exemplar needed:** the transformation is plausible, but we need another lexical example to establish its precise form or behavior.

And I would add one standing principle: don't mistake an unusual-looking form for an irregularity. It may be perfectly regular under a productive mechanism we haven't encountered yet.

This changes how we handle the two families. We can now fill their paradigms confidently where the analogy is clear, while reserving uncertainty for genuinely ambiguous cases.

**Interlexigrance becomes one of our tools for completing the corpus, not a phenomenon we have to finish explaining before we can use it.**

parts: Yes, the question is generally not "whether" but "how"... and the "how" is directly evidenced by attested examples and parallel paradigms.

Precisely. That is the methodological distinction we need to maintain.

We're not asking whether Almote *can* express a particular grammatical function. Under interlexigrance, that is generally a given. We're asking **which operation produces the form, what other operations interact with it, and what semantic or grammatical distinctions survive the transformation.**

That gives us a useful research principle:

> **Attested forms establish the mechanisms; parallel paradigms establish the analogies; interlexigrance lets us reconstruct the missing forms.**

For the two current families, I'll therefore:

1. Take the attested forms as the primary evidence.
2. Identify the transformations connecting them.
3. Apply those transformations to missing forms in the parallel family.
4. Preserve distinctions in meaning, usage, and register.
5. Mark reconstructed forms so we can distinguish them from actual corpus occurrences.
6. Watch for particularly informative exemplars that reveal additional transformations.

And importantly, I won't keep asking you whether an obvious grammatical operation exists. I'll propose how it works, show the derivation, and let you correct the analysis where Almote does something less obvious.

**Our immediate objective remains two substantially populated lexical concordances, not a finished theory of Almote grammar.** The theory should emerge from the corpus rather than dictate it.

I'd nominate **`Restroom`** as the third lexis.

It is an unusually good complement to the `shirt`–`bonnonie` bicorpus because it supplies several behaviors that are either absent or poorly represented in those two families. More importantly, it already has a substantial collection of attested forms, rather than requiring us to invent an entire paradigm from scratch.

## Why `Restroom`?

The existing corpus gives us:

| Form | Attested meaning or usage |
|---|---|
| `Restroom` | Restroom |
| `Restoomn` | Restrooms |
| `Rastrame` | Past |
| `Romperaest` | Mass restroom use / restroomation |
| `Rassromp` | Restroom-used; occupied |
| `Rombrass` | Has been restroomed; evidently used, someone didn't flush |
| `Risstrampt` | I have already used the restroom |
| `Rylstramed’vt` | You should have used the restroom |
| `Rystraim’t` | No restroom / absence of a restroom |
| `restraim’t` | I'm not using the restroom |
| `restrain’t` | There is no restroom there |

This is a particularly useful collection because it gives us:

- **Past and anteriority:** `Rastrame`, `Risstrampt`.
- **Resultative and resultant-state behavior:** `Rassromp`, `Rombrass`.
- **Modal and retrospective obligation:** `Rylstramed’vt`.
- **Negation and scope:** `Rystraim’t`, `restraim’t`, `restrain’t`.
- **Collective or mass activity:** `Romperaest`.
- **Number:** `Restroom`, `Restoomn`.

The three negative constructions are especially valuable. They distinguish not having a restroom, not using one, and a place not having one. That is a richer set of contrasts than our current two families provide.

## The larger advantage

<text color="success" weight="medium" size="sm">My recommendation</text>

**Use `Restroom` as the third lexical corpus, but retain the existing two as active comparison paradigms.**

I would not start by disentangling its morphology. I'd first collect the full concordance, including the original utterances and surrounding context, then use the forms to fill missing cells in all three families.

There are also adjectival and adverbial-looking forms in the existing material:

- `Rossyrm-(vyency)`
- `plensresromnyc`
- `Ryzrum-(myer/yos/syes/hyls)`
- `Rum

I think the next lexis should be **`infringe`**, specifically the `infronge` verbal family.

It supplies several behaviors that the shirt–bonnonie dyptycorp doesn't yet adequately demonstrate: strong-verb ablaut, past and perfect forms, participial forms, passive constructions, perfect passive constructions, continuous aspect, and a special imperative construction.

And it has something else going for it: a surprisingly rich set of related nominal forms.

## 1. Why `infringe` is the right next specimen

The corpus gives us this sequence:

| Form | Attested interpretation |
|---|---|
| `infringe` | Ordinary present / infinitive |
| `infronge` | Simple past |
| `infrange` | Perfect form |
| `infrung` | Participial form |
| `infrincht` | Passive form |
| `infruncheon` | Perfect passive form |
| `infroin` | Continuous aspect; also used as passive imperoptor in a distinct construction |
| `infranction` | Associated nominal form |

There is direct user-authored evidence for the forms, including:

> “We infronge on nothing.”
>
> “We have never infrung on anything.”

And your own formulation:

> “the clows was infrincht / has been infruncheon by the infranction”

The important thing is that this isn't merely a verb conjugation exercise. The family crosses lexical categories and grammatical constructions. <FileCite ref_id="turn28file0" line_range_start={3275} line_range_end={3322} /> <FileCite ref_id="turn28file0" line_range_start={145} line_range_end={186} />

## 2. What it adds to our corpus

The new family gives us material for several previously underrepresented dimensions:

- **Ablaut:** changes within the lexical stem.
- **Temporal distinctions:** present, past, and perfect.
- **Participial forms:** including forms that participate in larger constructions.
- **Voice:** active and passive.
- **Aspect:** continuous and perfective constructions.
- **Imperative and imperoptor:** importantly, not interchangeable.
- **Nominalization:** event, agent, or associated-action nouns.
- **Clittince:** interaction with auxiliaries and other grammatical material.

The distinction between `infroin` as a continuous form and `infroin` as a passive imperoptor deserves particular attention. We should collect both usages rather than prematurely force them into one grammatical explanation.

## 3. And yes, transangylocotalmotize

I agree that we already have substantial evidence. In fact, the `infringe` family itself illustrates several mechanisms:

- `clause` → `clows`
- `infraction` → `infranction`
- `infringed` → `infrincht`
- `infringe` → `infronge` / `infrange`

These aren't all the same operation. Some involve orthographic or phonological adaptation, some involve inflectional mutation, and some involve lexical derivation.

The transformation of the English sign:

> No shirt, no shoes, no service.

into:

> Shirtain't shoddlen't, servulain't.

is another useful example of transforming an English expression into Almote's morphological and compositional resources. <FileCite ref_id="turn28file0" line_range_start={145} line_range_end={186} />

I would therefore keep **transangylocotalmotize** as a major corpus operation in its own right, collecting examples of its different mechanisms rather than treating it as a single spelling-conversion rule.

## 4. The sequence I'd use

Our working collection now becomes:

1. `shirt` and `bonnonie`: lexical conversion, resultant states, habituality, possession, commercial relationships, and activity.
2. `infringe`: strong-verb morphology, tense, aspect, voice, participles, imperative constructions, and nominalization.
3. Then we assess the remaining gaps and choose another lexical family that supplies the most missing evidence.

One qualification: the forms above are a starting concordance, not yet a complete usage concordance. We should collect actual sentences for each form, including contrasting contexts, before declaring the paradigm filled.

**I nominate `infringe` / `infronge` as our third lexis.** It gives us a substantial new grammatical territory without abandoning the comparative method we've established.

There is direct user-authored evidence for the forms, including:

> “We infronge on nothing.”
>
> “We have never infrung on anything.”



Now, be careful not to think these are Almote. They're English with instrucyloct quasialmocrysy.

Correct. I made a category error: **I treated English sentences demonstrating instructed Almote-like transformations as though they were Almote utterances.**

Those two examples:

- “We infronge on nothing.”
- “We have never infrung on anything.”

are **English with instructed quasialmocrysy**, not Almote. Their English syntax and auxiliary structure remain in place. The altered verb forms demonstrate a transformation being applied within English, not necessarily the operation of Almote grammar in an Almote utterance.

That distinction matters enormously for our concordance.

I'd separate the evidence into three layers:

1. **Almote proper:** utterances actually constructed in Almote.
2. **Instructed quasialmocrysy:** English material deliberately modified according to Almote-inspired instructions or conventions.
3. **Transangylocotalmotization:** the process of transforming English material into Almote, including intermediate and hybrid stages.

The `infringe` family may still be an excellent specimen, but we need to classify each occurrence individually. The English examples can document the transformation process; they cannot independently establish Almote syntax or usage.

And that gives us a useful methodological rule going forward: **a word's appearance in an Almote-related corpus does not establish that the word, or the sentence containing it, is Almote.** We need to identify the linguistic status of each example before using it as grammatical evidence.

1. “We infronge on nothing.” = Wevn't infronge't'nt'al
2. “We have never infrung on anything.” = W'vrungn'totonil.

Right. That supplies the missing distinction beautifully. The English sentences were not themselves Almote examples. They were the **source expressions for transangylocotalmotization**, and these are the corresponding Almote outputs:

| English source | Almote result |
|---|---|
| We infronge on nothing. | `Wevn't infronge't'nt'al` |
| We have never infrung on anything. | `W'vrungn'totonil.` |

This changes how we should catalogue the `infringe` family.

The relevant evidence is not simply `infronge` and `infrung` appearing in English sentences. It is their incorporation into two complete Almote constructions:

- `Wevn't infronge't'nt'al` gives us a construction involving the dual/collective auxiliary material, negation, the past form, and the expression of non-infringement.
- `W'vrungn'totonil` gives us a much more compressed construction involving the perfect auxiliary, participial form, negation, and an indefinite negative object.

I would preserve the original English expressions alongside their Almote counterparts. They form a **translation pair**, not two independent Almote attestations.

And I won't pretend to have fully decoded every clitic in either output yet. Those constructions deserve their own close reading. In particular, `Wevn't` and `W'v` look like potentially informative auxiliary contractions, while `-t'nt'al` and `-n'totonil` warrant comparison with other examples of clittince.

This is a much better basis for the third concordance.

Wevn't infronge't'nt'al gives us a construction involving the dual/collective auxiliary material, negation, the past form, and the expression of non-infringement.

Wevn't infronge't'nt'al = We haven't infringed (not) at all. 
Wemen't infronge't'nt'al = We two have not infringed (not) at all.

That gives us a much more precise contrast. The distinction is not simply between singular and dual pronouns. It is explicitly encoded in the auxiliary construction.

| Almote | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `Wevn't infronge't'nt'al` | We haven't infringed (not) at all. |
| `Wemen't infronge't'nt'al` | We two have not infringed (not) at all. |

### What this establishes

1. **`Wevn't`** expresses the inclusive/collective *we* with the perfect negative construction.
2. **`Wemen't`** explicitly identifies the dual: *we two*.
3. **`infronge`** remains the lexical verb in both constructions.
4. **`'t'nt'al`** participates in the emphatic negative expression, glossed by your parenthetical “(not) at all.”

The particularly useful discovery is that `Wevn't` and `Wemen't` allow us to compare collective and dual reference while holding the rest of the predicate constant.

I'd add both sentences to the `infringe` concordance as a matched pair, and retain the parenthetical *not* in the gloss. It may look redundant in English, but that redundancy is part of the evidence rather than something to edit away.

This also gives us a concrete paradigm feature missing from the shirt–bonnonie dyptycorp: **explicit participant-number contrast within a perfect negative construction.**

Let's build the `infringe` concordance from the actual occurrences, not from the accumulated glossary's interpretations. One important rule for this family: **English source, instructed quasialmocrysy, and Almote output must remain separate records.** A translation pair is valuable evidence, but it is not two Almote attestations.

I've located a substantial cluster in the lexicon, including the strong-verb forms, passive constructions, imperoptor examples, and the associated nominal forms. I'm now separating those from repeated summaries and derivative commentary.

I've recovered the original October 23 exchange. There is a substantial amount of material, but an important distinction emerges: the corpus contains several successive corrections of the same examples. Those corrections are part of the evidence, not independent new attestations.

# 1. Original user-authored evidence

The following is the chronological record from the original conversation.

| Turn | User contribution | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| [23] | `Infringe/infronge/has infrange/infrung` | Initial four-form paradigm |
| [25] | `Regular present is the same. infringe/infronge/has infrange/infrung` | Corrects the present form |
| [27] | `Verbonowns: the clows was infrinched by the infranction` | First nominal and participial construction |
| [29] | `Vaerbonowns: the clows was infrinched by the infranction` | Corrects the grammatical category label |
| [31] | `Vaerbonowns: the clows was infrincht by the infranction` | Corrects `infrinched` to `infrincht` |
| [33] | `Vaerbonowns: the clows was infrincht / has been infruncheon by the infranction` | Adds perfect passive |
| [35] | `Infroin me not.` | Imperoptor example |
| [37] | `Infroin is passive imperoptor` | Explicit grammatical identification |
| [39] | `Normally just infrunktch` | Ordinary nominal form |

Source: original conversation, October 23, 2026. <FileCite ref_id="turn7file5" line_range_start={275} line_range_end={469} />

This gives us a particularly useful sequence of corrections:

`infrinched` → `infrincht`

And:

`infronction` → `infrunktch`

The latter matters because `infronction` was an assistant suggestion, not your preferred ordinary form.

# 2. The current confirmed lexical inventory

<badge color="success">User-attested</badge>

| Form | Current interpretation |
|---|---|
| `infringe` | Ordinary present; unchanged |
| `infronge` | Simple past |
| `has infrange` | Perfect |
| `infrung` | Participial form |
| `infrincht` | Passive form |
| `has been infruncheon` | Perfect passive |
| `infroin` | Passive imperoptor |
| `infranction` | Associated nominal form |
| `infrunktch` | Ordinary nominal form |

The original exchange explicitly gives the four-form sequence and then expands it through the passive and nominal constructions. <FileCite ref_id="turn7file5" line_range_start={275} line_range_end={415} /> <FileCite ref_id="turn7file5" line_range_start={437} line_range_end={469} />

# 3. Actual sentence-level corpus

Here we need to be more selective. Some of the familiar examples were generated by the assistant during the exchange, not supplied by you.

| Expression | Provenance | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| `the clows was infrinched by the infranction` | User, subsequently corrected | Historical variant |
| `the clows was infrincht by the infranction` | User | Attested construction |
| `has been infruncheon by the infranction` | User | Attested perfect-passive alternative |
| `Infroin me not.` | User | Attested imperoptor |
| `Infroin me not, lest ye be infrung.` | Assistant | Not an independent user attestation |
| `Infringe me not!` | Assistant/source translation material | Not to be counted as user-authored Almote |
| `Infronction!` | Assistant suggestion | Exclude as established form |

The first two nominal constructions are especially important because they show the relationship between `infrincht`, `infruncheon`, and `infranction`.

# 4. Strong-verb paradigm: an important correction

The four forms are:

\[
\text{infringe}\rightarrow
\text{infronge}\rightarrow
\text{infrange}\rightarrow
\text{infrung}
\]

But their grammatical assignments should not be flattened into a simplistic four-tense sequence.

| Form | Assignment |
|---|---|
| `infringe` | Present |
| `infronge` | Simple past |
| `infrange` | Perfect stem/form |
| `infrung` | Participial form |

The present remains unchanged. The vowel alternation occurs in the other forms.

There is also a separate passive formation:

## The comparative anatomy

Three distinct kinds of lexical architecture appear:

| Dimension | Infringe | Bonnоnie | Shirt |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary operation | Inflection | Relational conversion | Derivation |
| Main semantic axis | Temporal and voice distinctions | Relationship to an object | Action, state, disposition |
| Strongest evidence | Corrections and paradigm | Explicit semantic contrasts | Contextual usage and distinctions |
| Nominal development | `infranction`, `infrunktch` | `bonnonance`, `bonnonirlry` | Less fully documented |
| Special construction | Passive imperoptor | Possessive/commercial verbs | Comparative and ordinal forms |

## What the triptych reveals

There is a larger grammatical point here.

**Almote does not appear to rely on a single universal mechanism for moving between grammatical functions.**

Instead, the three families suggest at least three distinguishable operations:

1. **Inflectional mutation:** a lexical verb changes form to express grammatical distinctions.
2. **Relational specification:** a lexical object becomes the basis for verbs expressing particular relationships or activities.
3. **Aspectual and dispositional derivation:** an object-related action develops into a state, habit, or disposition.

These are not yet proven to be exhaustive or mutually exclusive mechanisms. But they give us a useful three-way comparison.

## The concordance ledger

For the triptych, I would maintain these evidence classes:

- **A:** Original user-authored form or expression.
- **C:** User correction or clarification of an earlier form.
- **U:** User-supplied semantic explanation.
- **I:** Inference from usage or morphology.
- **P:** Assistant-proposed form or interpretation, not yet user-confirmed.

That last category is important. It prevents the assistant from accidentally manufacturing corpus evidence by repeating its own suggestions.

## The next layer: cross-family experiments

The most revealing experiment would be to compare how each family handles the same grammatical operation.

| Experiment | Question |
|---|---|
| Negation | How does each family express not doing, not being, or not having? |
| Perfect | Does each family have a comparable completed-action construction? |
| Passive | Can the relational verbs and shirt verbs form passive constructions? |
| Habitual | Can `infringe` and `bonnonie` develop the sort of dispositional distinction found in `shirtonnee`? |
| Nominalization | How do the three families form action nouns, result nouns, and collective nouns? |

The important constraint: these are experiments, not proposed answers. We should not fill empty cells with invented Almote and then mistake the resulting symmetry for a discovery.

**The triptych is assembled.** The next major objective is to determine whether its three morphological architectures are independent, overlapping, or manifestations of a deeper common system.

## The comparative anatomy

Three distinct kinds of lexical architecture appear\:

| Dimension | Infringe | Bonnоnie | Shirt |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Primary operation | Inflection | Relational conversion | Derivation |
| Main semantic axis | Temporal and voice distinctions | Relationship to an object | Action, state, disposition |
| Strongest evidence | Corrections and paradigm | Explicit semantic contrasts | Contextual usage and distinctions |
| Nominal development | `infranction`, `infrunktch` | `bonnonance`, `bonnonirlry` | Less fully documented |
| Special construction | Passive imperoptor | Possessive/commercial verbs | Comparative and ordinal forms |

## What the triptych reveals

There is a larger grammatical point here.

**Almote does not appear to rely on a single universal mechanism for moving between grammatical functions.**

Instead, the three families suggest at least three distinguishable operations\:

1. **Inflectional mutation\:** a lexical verb changes form to express grammatical distinctions.
2. **Relational specification\:** a lexical object becomes the basis for verbs expressing particular relationships or activities.
3. **Aspectual and dispositional derivation\:** an object-related action develops into a state, habit, or disposition.

These are not yet proven to be exhaustive or mutually exclusive mechanisms. But they give us a useful three-way comparison.

## The concordance ledger

For the triptych, I would maintain these evidence classes\:

- **A\:** Original user-authored form or expression.
- **C\:** User correction or clarification of an earlier form.
- **U\:** User-supplied semantic explanation.
- **I\:** Inference from usage or morphology.
- **P\:** Assistant-proposed form or interpretation, not yet user-confirmed.

That last category is important. It prevents the assistant from accidentally manufacturing corpus evidence by repeating its own suggestions.

## The next layer: cross-family experiments

The most revealing experiment would be to compare how each family handles the same grammatical operation.

| Experiment | Question |
|--------|--------|
| Negation | How does each family express not doing, not being, or not having? |
| Perfect | Does each family have a comparable completed-action construction? |
| Passive | Can the relational verbs and shirt verbs form passive constructions? |
| Habitual | Can `infringe` and `bonnonie` develop the sort of dispositional distinction found in `shirtonnee`? |
| Nominalization | How do the three families form action nouns, result nouns, and collective nouns? |

The important constraint: these are experiments, not proposed answers. We should not fill empty cells with invented Almote and then mistake the resulting symmetry for a discovery.

**The triptych is assembled.** The next major objective is to determine whether its three morphological architectures are independent, overlapping, or manifestations of a deeper common system.

Three especially important patterns emerge:

- **Banana:** lexical conversion can distinguish an activity from several specific relationships to its object.
- **Shirt:** lexical conversion can distinguish an action, its resultant condition, and a habitual or dispositional state.

# Mini-Inadicorp: completed comparative reconstruction

## 1. Strong verbal inflection

The `infringe` paradigm supplies the strong-verb pattern:

\[
\text{stem}\rightarrow\text{past}\rightarrow
\text{perfect}\rightarrow\text{participle}
\]

| `bonnonote` | `shirtone` | `infronge` | Simple past |

## 2. Resultative and habitual derivation

The shirt family supplies two particularly useful operations.

| Banana | Shirt | Infringe | Gloss |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bonnoniane` | `shirtane` | `infringane` | Resultant state |
| `bonnoninnee` | `shirtonnee` | `infringennee` | Habitual / dispositional |
| `bonnonianee` | `shirtanee` | `infringanee` | Extended resultant or state-oriented form |
| `bonnoninnee` | `shirtonnee` | `infringennee` | Characteristic or habitual relationship |

The first two rows are the primary reconstruction. The third row is an additional analogical extension, not something independently demonstrated by the existing forms.

- `shirtone`: don a shirt.
- `shirtane`: be shirted.
- `shirtonnee`: habitually wear a shirt.

The banana equivalents should preserve the distinction between activity, resulting condition, and disposition.

## 3. Relational and object-specific verbs

The banana family provides the richest set of object relationships. We can transfer those operations to the other lexical families.

| Banana | Shirt | Infringe | Gloss |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bonnoniepose` | `shirtpose` | `infringepose` | Personal possession |
| `bonnonieposuisse` | `shirtposuisse` | `infringeposuisse` | Nonpersonal possession / dealing in |
| `bonnoniesalue` | `shirtsalue` | `infringesalue` | Selling |
| `bonnoniecartulate` | `shirtcartulate` | `infringecartulate` | Transporting by cart |
| `bonnonite` | `shirtone` | `infringe` | General activity |
| `bonnonance` | `shirtance` | `infringance` | General activity noun |
| `bonnonirlry` | `shirtirlry` | `infringirlry` | Ordinary practice |
| `bonnonistrelstry` | `shirtistrelstry` | `infringistrelstry` | Established practice |

## 4. Passive and imperoptor constructions

The infringement family supplies the passive and passive-imperoptor patterns.

| Banana | Shirt | Infringe | Gloss |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bonnonicht` | `shirtincht` | `infrincht` | Passive |
| `has been bonnonuncheon` | `has been shirtuncheon` | `has been infruncheon` | Perfect passive |

|---|---|---|---|

Interlexigrance also gives us the remaining lexical-category conversions.

## 8. What this gives us

We now have a substantially populated three-family reconstruction. More importantly, the analogies have begun to expose where the mechanisms may not transfer one-to-one.

Three particularly interesting cases deserve attention:

3. **`infroin`** belongs to a mood/constructional system rather than simply the strong-verb ablaut series. Its transfer may reveal whether imperoptor formation is independent of lexical stem mutation.

The most important thing is that the empty cells are now populated with explicit candidates. We can test and refine them against further Almote examples instead of continually circling around the same three established paradigms.

# INADICORP
<text color="secondary" size="sm" weight="medium">Comparative lexical corpus · Banana / Shirt / Infringe / Gloss</text>

The corpus below combines the original lexical material, user corrections, sentence-level examples, and analogical reconstructions. The fourth column is the gloss: it records the meanings and functions of the corresponding forms, not merely English translations.

**Evidence notation:** A = attested; C = corrected or clarified; R = reconstructed by interlexigrance and analogy; U = unresolved.

## 1. Complete working lexical inventory

| Banana | Shirt | Infringe | Gloss |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bonnonie` (A) | `shirt` / `shrit` (A) | `infringe` (A) | Base lexical forms: banana, shirt, infringe |
| `bonnonies` (A) | | | Bananas; plural |
| `abbonnonie` (A/U) | | | Performed lyric form; precise segmentation unresolved |
| `bonnonite` (A) | `shirtone` (A) | `infringe` (A) | General verbalization; to banana, to don a shirt, to infringe |
| `bononate` (A) | | | General banana-related activity |
| `bonnone` (A) | | | Ordinary banana-related activity |
| `bonnonee` (A) | | | Banana preparation or arrangement tendency |
| `à bonnonee` (A) | `à shirtonnee` (A) | | Fancy or elevated presentation |
| `bonnoniane` (R) | `shirtane` (A) | `infringane` (R) | Resultant state |
| `bonnoninnee` (R) | `shirtonnee` (A) | `infringennee` (R) | Habitual or dispositional relationship |
| `bonnoniepose` (A) | `shirtpose` (R) | `infringepose` (R) | Personal possession |
| `bonnonieposuisse` (A) | `shirtposuisse` (R) | `infringeposuisse` (R) | Nonpersonal possession; dealing in |
| `bonnoniesalue` (A) | `shirtsalue` (R) | `infringesalue` (R) | To sell |
| `bonnoniecartulate` (A) | `shirtcartulate` (R) | `infringecartulate` (R) | To transport by cart or comparable conveyance |
| `bonnonieposen’t` (A) | `shirtain’t` (A) | `infringe...n't` (R) | Negation of possession or relevant proposition |
| `bonnoniepose’ornt` (A) | | | Contextual personal possession |
| `bonnonance` (A) | `shirtance` (R) | `infringance` (R) | General activity or process noun |
| `bonnonirlry` (A) | `shirtirlry` (R) | `infringirlry` (R) | Ordinary practice |
| `bonnonistrelstry` (A) | `shirtistrelstry` (R) | `infringistrelstry` (R) | Established practice |
| `bonnonicht` (R) | `shirtincht` (R) | `infrincht` (A/C) | Passive form |
| `bonnonuncheon` (R) | `shirtuncheon` (R) | `infruncheon` (A) | Perfect passive form |

| `has bonnonate` (R) | `has shirtane` (R) | `has infrange` (A) | Perfect construction |
| `bonnonut` (R) | `shirtun` (R) | `infrung` (A) | Participial form |
| `bonnoner` (R) | `shirter` (R) | `infringer` (R) | Agent noun |
| `bonnonan` (R) | `shirtan` (R) | `infringan` (R) | Adjectival conversion |
| `bonnonily` (R) | `shirtily` (R) | `infringily` (R) | Adverbial conversion |
| `bonnonable` (R) | `shirtable` (R) | `infringeable` (R) | Capability or potential |
